solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Hint about desire, dropping head in mischievous way

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so IMPLY is wrapped around the other piece
to drop your head is to let the top fall away, so WISH loses its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone hints that they want something, then loses their nerve and turns to mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mischievous' alone would be an adjective; the definition has to run to 'in mischievous way' to match an adverb ending in -LY.
explanation.definitionFit: Impishly means in the manner of an imp, that is, mischievously.

clue.text: Part of foot I note and measure

blocks.note: a step is a measure, as in 'take steps'

explanation.surface: A podiatrist jots down a note and measures part of a patient's foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' looks like a verb for the podiatrist; here it is the noun, a step taken to get something done.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the arch between toes and ankle is one named region of the foot.

clue.text: Implement persuasive proposal aimed at kids primarily

indicators.note: take only the first letter of 'kids'

blocks.note: a product aimed at kids is for kids

explanation.surface: An instruction to put into effect a marketing pitch targeted at children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Implement' sits at the front as a verb, as if telling someone to carry out the proposal; it is the noun, a tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitchfork is a farm implement for lifting hay.

clue.text: Odd stone assortment

blocks.note: ST = stone, the British unit of weight (14 lb)
a range of goods is an assortment

explanation.surface: An odd-looking mix of stones, perhaps in a garden or a jeweller's tray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd stone' reads as one unusual pebble; 'Odd' is the definition and 'stone' is the weight, still used in Britain for body weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Strange and odd both mean unusual.

clue.text: Nimble and cheerful, dismissing opener

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is sent away

explanation.surface: A cricketer who is quick and upbeat despite the opening batsman being out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opener' suggests a cricket opener; here it is just the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithe means supple and agile, so nimble.

clue.text: Source of wisdom, core of work by expert absorbing learner

indicators.note: take the middle letters of 'work'
a sponge absorbing water takes it inside, so ACE takes L into its middle

blocks.note: L = learner, from the L-plates on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A mentor's wisdom comes from the heart of a craftsman's work as he teaches an apprentice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Source of wisdom' is the definition, not a hint at 'core'; the clue reads as one long phrase, so find where the wordplay starts.
explanation.definitionFit: An oracle is a person or shrine consulted for wise answers.

clue.text: Copy of criticism

blocks.note: a repro is a reproduction, a copy

explanation.surface: A photocopy of a critical review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' looks like a link joining two halves; it is itself part of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a reproof is a telling-off, the spoken form of criticism.

clue.text: Fragment containing right sound of bird

indicators.note: a box containing something holds it inside, so CHIP holds R

blocks.note: a chip is a small broken piece

explanation.surface: A piece of recording that captures the correct birdsong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right sound' reads as the correct sound; 'right' is just R, and 'sound of bird' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A chirp is the short high sound a small bird makes.

clue.text: Unabridged condition in statement I retyped

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the next words

explanation.surface: A typist confirms a document was retyped in full, without cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retyped' tempts you toward an anagram, but the letters simply run in order across three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in its entirety is whole and uncut, unabridged.

clue.text: Stupid person nearly damaged water pumps?

indicators.note: nearly a word is all of it but not quite, so the last letter goes
the letters of 'water' are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A fool has broken the water pumps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water pumps' reads as machinery; the question mark flags that pumps are light shoes, an example of footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Pumps are light slip-on shoes, one kind of footwear.

clue.text: Jostling on a train, up to its full capacity level

indicators.note: the letters push about into a new order

blocks.clueFragment: on a train, up to its

anagrams.fodder: ON A TRAIN UP TO ITS

explanation.surface: Commuters shoving on a train packed right to the limit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a rush-hour carriage, which is exactly a train at saturation point.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturation point is the level at which nothing more can be taken in.

clue.text: Intensify act of punishment, losing power to capture hearts

indicators.note: something losing a part no longer has it, so PENANCE gives up its P
to capture is to take prisoner and hold inside, so ENANCE holds H

explanation.surface: A harsher penalty is imposed, although the authorities give up power to win hearts.
explanation.walkthrough: P = power is standard in physics. 'Capture hearts' reads as winning affection; it only asks for the card-suit letter to be held.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean make stronger, as in enhancing or intensifying a flavour.

clue.text: Love getting into story about soldier

indicators.note: getting into a car puts you inside it, so O goes inside the other piece
to turn about is to face the other way, so REPORT is written backwards

blocks.note: O = love, a zero score in tennis

explanation.surface: A romance story centred on a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love getting into story' suggests a romance plot; love is only the letter O, and the story is a news report.
explanation.definitionFit: A trooper is a private soldier, originally in a cavalry or armoured unit.

clue.text: Possibly rib hero, reportedly very lazy

indicators.note: a rib is one example of a bone
'idol' said out loud gives IDLE

explanation.surface: Someone may tease a hero who, by all accounts, is terribly lazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rib' looks like the verb to tease; it is the bone. Bone idle is a British phrase for utterly lazy.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'bone' works as an intensifier, as in bone dry, so the phrase is idle through and through.

clue.text: Ban I had, climbing tree

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up reverses I'D

blocks.note: a sallow is a kind of willow tree

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they were banned for climbing a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbing tree' paints a child up a tree; 'climbing' works on I'D, and the tree is SALLOW, a low willow.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a referee who disallows a goal bans it from counting.

clue.text: Church seen in profitable aspect

indicators.note: something seen in a place is found within it, so CE sits inside FAT

blocks.note: a fat profit, a fat contract

explanation.surface: The church has been spotted in a money-making role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Profitable' has to shrink to a three-letter word; fat, as in a fat fee, is the informal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the cut faces of a gem: each facet is one aspect you can look at.

clue.text: Fraud with offer for candidate

blocks.note: to tender is to offer, as in tendering a bid

explanation.surface: A swindler makes an offer on behalf of an election candidate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply puts CON beside TENDER.
explanation.definitionFit: A contender is a candidate competing for a post or prize.

clue.text: Poor weapon stops having weight evenly distributed

indicators.note: LANCE plugs the gap in BAD

blocks.note: a lance is a knight's spear

explanation.surface: A badly made weapon stops being well balanced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stops' reads as ceases; it is the sense of stopping up a hole, the way a cork stops a bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description, the literal sense of a pair of scales sitting level.

clue.text: Crooked request we rejected

indicators.note: WE is sent back, so turned round

explanation.surface: A dishonest request that we turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crooked' reads as dishonest; it is the physical sense, not straight.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the physical sense: a picture hanging askew is hanging crooked.

clue.text: Call for conflict and speak wildly

blocks.note: to rant is to speak wildly

explanation.surface: A demagogue calls for war and shouts wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call for' looks like one phrase; 'Call' alone is the definition, as in 'there is no call for that'.
explanation.definitionFit: Call and warrant both mean justification: no call for it, no warrant for it.

clue.text: Examination endlessly clean and minute

indicators.note: SCRUB loses its last letter

explanation.surface: An inspection that never ends, checking for cleanliness down to the last minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as a unit of time; it is the adjective meaning very small.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an account under scrutiny is under close inspection.

clue.text: Temper from thug one maddened

indicators.note: the letters are driven wild, so rearranged

explanation.surface: A bad temper from a thug who has been driven mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temper' reads as the noun, anger; it is the verb used of steel, to harden it.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical sense: tempered glass and tempered steel have been heat-treated to make them harder.

clue.text: River delta far south of Maine

indicators.note: in a down entry, DWAY comes below ME

blocks.note: ME = Maine, the US state abbreviation
D = delta in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A river delta lying well to the south of the state of Maine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Medway is a river in Kent, south-east England. 'River delta' reads as one thing; 'River' is the definition and 'delta' the letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: The Medway is an English river flowing into the Thames estuary.

clue.text: Outrage going round about habit?

indicators.note: a fence going round a field encloses it, so APPAL wraps around RE

blocks.note: re = about, as in memo headers

explanation.surface: Indignation that circles round a routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' reads as a routine; the question mark flags that it is an example of clothing, a nun's habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit, like a monk's, is a kind of apparel.

clue.text: Italian food in former time first-class

blocks.note: A = first-class, as in A1 or an A grade

explanation.surface: Italian cooking of the old days was excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: Unusually, 'in' is the link: the answer is found in the wordplay that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain category: spaghetti, penne and the rest are the Italian food most people know.

clue.text: Kip in small cabin unknown in middle of freeze

indicators.note: what is in something sits inside it, so Y goes between the two Es
take the central letters of 'freeze'

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
a hut is a small cabin
x, y, z are algebra's unknowns
the two middle letters of frEEze

explanation.surface: A nap in a little hut, out in the middle of a big freeze.
explanation.walkthrough: Kip is British slang for sleep. EE opens to take Y, making EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: Shut-eye and kip are both informal words for sleep.

clue.text: Spot quote in speech

indicators.note: the answer is how 'cite' sounds when spoken

blocks.note: to quote a source is to cite it

explanation.surface: Picking out a quotation in someone's talk.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'Spot' and 'quote' can be verbs or nouns; the definition is the verb, to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sailors who sight land have spotted it.

clue.text: Actors, mostly isolated by good playwright holding party, have lasting influence

indicators.note: drop the last letter of ALONE
holding something means keeping it in your grasp, so SHAW keeps DO inside

blocks.note: the actors in a play are its cast

explanation.surface: A cast left stranded by a fine dramatist who throws a party still leaves its mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good playwright' reads as a compliment; 'good' is just G, and the playwright is Shaw, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that casts a long shadow goes on affecting things long afterwards.

clue.text: Lack thread to spin

indicators.note: the letters whirl into a new order

explanation.surface: A spinner has run out of yarn to work with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thread to spin' is a spinner's raw material, and 'spin' is also the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a dearth of rain is a lack of it.

clue.text: Twit’s taken aback by poet’s name for fish

indicators.note: 'aback' means backwards, so what is taken aback is written in reverse

blocks.note: NIT'S (a nit is a twit) turned round
Thomas Gray, author of the Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard

explanation.surface: A fool is startled by what a poet calls a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken aback' reads as surprised; it means turned back. A nit is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A stingray is a flat fish with a venomous tail spine.
